parts.label: a · x coordinate of center of mass
parts.explanation: Equal masses give the arithmetic mean of the x coordinates.

parts.label: b · y coordinate of center of mass
parts.explanation: Equal masses give the arithmetic mean of the y coordinates.

parts.label: c · x coordinate of center of gravity
parts.explanation: Weight each x coordinate by the local gravitational acceleration; common mass cancels.

parts.explanation: Use Σgᵢyᵢ/Σgᵢ, not the unweighted center of mass.

reasoning: COM=(Σx/6,Σy/6); COG=(Σg x/Σg,Σg y/Σg), using all six g values and coordinates in Fig.12-25. Verification: Weight sums are 46.2 in common units; all weighted positions lie inside the 0–2 m by 0–4 m rectangle.

parts.label: a · Force on each front wheel

reasoning: Rear axle torque: Nrear×3.05=W×1.78; front+rear=W. Verification: Both axle loads sum to 13328 N, and the rear-axle moment equals the weight moment.

reasoning: T L/√(L²+r²)=mg; N=T r/√(L²+r²)=mgr/L. Verification: The computed tension has vertical component 8.33 N; its horizontal component equals the wall force.

Yes, torque balance at O guarantees it at A
No, it can never balance about A

parts.answer: Not necessarily; only if OB is parallel to the net force or the net force is zero
options: Not necessarily; only if OB is parallel to the net force or the net force is zero
Yes, torque balance at O guarantees it at B
No, it can never balance about B
parts.explanation: UseτB=τO−OB×Fnet.

parts.label: c · Must torque balance about C?
parts.answer: Not necessarily; only if OC is parallel to the net force or the net force is zero
options: Not necessarily; only if OC is parallel to the net force or the net force is zero
Yes, torque balance at O guarantees it at C
No, it can never balance about C
parts.explanation: An off-stick pivot also changes torque according to its displacement crossed with net force.

parts.label: d · If torque at O is nonzero, can another pivot balance it?
parts.answer: Yes if the net force is nonzero; no if the forces form a nonzero pure couple
options: Yes if the net force is nonzero; no if the forces form a nonzero pure couple
Always yes, even for a pure couple
Always no, regardless of the net force
parts.explanation: For coplanar forces withFnet≠0 one can choose an origin on the resultant force line of action. A pure couple has the same nonzero torque about everyorigin.

reasoning: The figure gives force directions but not magnitudes. Torque balance alone cannot establish translational equilibrium. Use the exact origin-shift law rather than silently assumeΣF=0. Verification: The torque-origin transformation follows directly by summing (ri−rP)×Fi; a pure couple tests and confirms the stated exception.
assumptions: Coplanar forces as shown; no force magnitudes or net-force condition are specified.
